svg.title: Characters & relationships
svg.desc: Macbeth’s transformation: “Brave Macbeth” (1.2) → secret desire → hesitation → murder → independent tyranny. “Fruitless crown” (3.1): power without secure inheritance. “Walking shadow” (5.5): achievement feels empty. Pity for wasted potential can coexist with condemnation. Lady Macbeth’s change: “Unsex me here” (1.5): she tries to suppress compassion. Challenges manhood; controls the plan. “A little water” (2.2) minimises guilt; sleepwalking and “damned spot” (5.1) expose its persistence. Her requests for cruelty can reveal vulnerability, not effortless evil. Marriage: power shifts: Act 1: “partner of greatness”; shared ambition. Act 2: she returns daggers and covers panic. Act 3: he plans Banquo’s death without her; she tries to protect his image at the banquet. Act 5: emotional isolation. He is not controlled by her throughout. Banquo & Macduff: Banquo is a foil: shares curiosity about prophecy but warns of deception; Fleance’s escape keeps Macbeth insecure. Macduff resists tyranny and grieves: “I must also feel it as a man” (4.3). His duty to Scotland conflicts painfully with family safety. Duncan & Malcolm: Duncan rewards service but misjudges loyalty. His trust makes Macbeth’s betrayal more disturbing. Malcolm tests Macduff before trusting him; responsible kingship contrasts with self-protection. Ending restores political order, without undoing suffering. Witches & innocents: Witches offer tempting predictions and double meanings; they never tell Macbeth to kill Duncan. Lady Macduff and her son make the cost of tyranny visible through domestic dialogue and stage violence. Fleance escapes; the play does not show his future kingship.
